venues.d: A former Inca palace turned convent, now an all-suite Belmond hideaway around a serene courtyard — Cusco's most refined address, with butler service and in-room oxygen.
A 16th-century monastery beside the cathedral — cloistered courtyards, a 300-year-old cedar and a gilded colonial chapel — the grande dame of Cusco.
A restored 16th-century convent moments from the Plaza de Armas — colonial cloisters, on-site Inca ruins and archaeology, wrapped around full modern luxury.
A 16th-century manor on a quiet plazoleta, Cusco's first Relais & Châteaux — just eleven suites of hand-restored colonial character around a private courtyard.
The only hotel at the gates of Machu Picchu — steps from the citadel entrance, letting members walk in at first light before the day crowds arrive.
Eighty whitewashed casitas in a private cloud-forest reserve by the river below the citadel — the loveliest, most naturalist base for Machu Picchu.
An all-inclusive lodge facing the Andes, built for exploration — guided hikes, bikes and Inca sites by day, and a restaurant with a menu shaped by Virgilio Martínez.

venues.n: Tambo del Inka, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa, Valle Sagrado
venues.d: A riverside resort in the heart of the valley — the only hotel with its own private station for the train to Machu Picchu, plus a heated indoor pool and spa.
Casitas scattered across a 37-acre garden estate, hung with contemporary Peruvian art — a characterful, colour-filled Relais & Châteaux in the valley floor.

venues.n: Palacio del Inka, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Cusco
venues.d: A 500-year-old mansion facing the Koricancha sun temple — grand colonial rooms, a spa and a serious pisco bar, a short walk from the Plaza de Armas.
Virgilio Martínez and Pía León's high-Andes restaurant above the Moray terraces — an eight-course journey through the ecosystems around it, at 3,600 m.
A candlelit colonial room above a tapas bar off the Plaza de Armas — Mediterranean technique on Andean produce, and for years the connoisseur's favourite table in Cusco.
A glass pavilion set in the courtyard of the Pre-Columbian Art Museum — refined, contemporary Peruvian cooking amid one of Cusco's finest collections.
Gastón Acurio's Cusco house on the Plaza Regocijo — regional Andean cooking, from cuy to alpaca and river trout, from Peru's most celebrated chef.
Meats and seafood seared at the table on volcanic hot stones, just off the Plaza de Armas — interactive, generous and a firm Cusco favourite.
The all-day café arm of Cicciolina — fresh bread, pastries and honest Andean-European plates in a bright, easy room off the main square.
Cusco's best Chifa — the Peruvian-Cantonese cooking born of Chinese migration — in a warm room near the Plaza Regocijo.
The elegant dining room of the JW Marriott convent hotel — modern Peruvian cooking with local produce, in colonial-cloister surrounds.
A long-running family kitchen serving Cusco's classic dishes — the slow-roasted cuy among them — done properly and without ceremony.
A garden restaurant in Urubamba named for the Andean herb — inventive Peruvian-fusion cooking that is the valley's most-loved fine table.

The most famous ruin on earth, and it earns it — a lost Inca city of terraces and temples riding a knife-edge ridge 2,430 metres up, with the green sugarloaf of Huayna Picchu behind and cloud drifting through the valley below. Timed circuit tickets and a licensed guide are now mandatory, so a private advisor books the first entry, the quietest circuit and a guide who paces it gently for grandparents. Arrive by the early train from Ollantaytambo to catch the citadel before the day-trippers.

The sheer green peak that towers behind every classic Machu Picchu photograph — a steep, exposed 2 to 3-hour scramble up Inca stairs to temples and terraces perched above the citadel, with a bird's-eye view straight down onto the ruins. Access is capped at a few hundred people a day on a separate timed ticket, so it must be secured months ahead. Not for vertigo or shaky knees; the gentler Machu Picchu Mountain is the multi-gen alternative.

The original Inca entrance to the sanctuary, set on a saddle above the citadel where the last day of the Inca Trail delivers trekkers at dawn for their first, breath-catching glimpse of Machu Picchu below. You can walk up to it from the ruins in about an hour and a half without any trek permit — a gentle, rewarding stroll that trades the crowds for silence and one of the great views in the Andes.

The pilgrim's road to Machu Picchu — four days over three high passes on original Inca-laid stone, through cloud forest and past ruins invisible from the train, ending at the Sun Gate at first light. Permits are strictly capped, sell out months ahead and cannot be bought day-of; a luxury operator runs it with private porters, a chef and proper tents. High and demanding — for fit travellers, with the one-day Km 104 version for those short on time.

The most glamorous way to reach Machu Picchu — a 1920s Pullman-style luxury train of polished wood and brass with brunch or a four-course dinner, a bar car, live Peruvian music and picture windows onto the Urubamba gorge. Fares run to several hundred dollars each way and include the bus up to the citadel and a guided tour. The effortless, elegant choice for a family who want the journey to feel like part of the treasure.

The workhorse route to Machu Picchu, and a lovely one — glass-roofed carriages from PeruRail and Inca Rail thread the Urubamba river gorge from Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes in about ninety minutes. The Vistadome and top-tier Sacred and 360° services add panoramic roofs, snacks and onboard performance. Staying in the Sacred Valley first, then boarding here, is the smart acclimatisation-friendly way to do Machu Picchu without the longer Cusco run.

The little cloud-forest town at the foot of the mountain where the trains terminate and the buses to the citadel depart — hemmed by jungle peaks and rushing river, with hot springs that give it its name. It is where families overnight to catch the first entry uphill next morning. Belmond's Sanctuary Lodge is the only hotel at the ruins themselves; in town, Inkaterra's cloud-forest reserve is the discreet luxury choice.

The beating heart of the old Inca capital and the finest colonial square in the Andes — arcaded stone balconies, two great churches and a fountain, ringed by peaks and lit gold at night, built directly over the Inca ceremonial plaza of Haucaypata. Sit on a first-floor balcony with a coffee or a pisco sour and watch the city move below. The natural anchor for a first, gentle acclimatisation day before anything strenuous.

The great Renaissance-Baroque cathedral on the plaza, raised over the Inca palace of Inca Wiracocha and filled with Cusco School canvases — including the famous 'Last Supper' where Christ and the apostles dine on guinea pig and Andean fruit. A private guide unlocks the silver altars, the choir stalls and the black-Christ El Señor de los Temblores, the city's protector. Cool, quiet and unhurried — easy on grandparents.

venues.n: Qorikancha (Temple of the Sun / Santo Domingo)
venues.d: The holiest temple of the Inca empire, once sheathed in sheets of gold, over which the Spanish built the church and convent of Santo Domingo — so you walk through baroque cloisters and suddenly meet flawless Inca stonework that has survived every earthquake since. No mortar, no gap you could slide paper into; the single clearest lesson in Inca genius in the city. A short, level visit near the centre.

A single diorite block cut with twelve precise angles to lock seamlessly into the wall of what was an Inca palace and is now the Archbishop's residence — the most photographed stone in Peru, a jeweller's-eye demonstration of masonry without mortar or metal tools. It sits on cobbled Hatun Rumiyoc street a few minutes' walk uphill from the plaza, on the pretty route to San Blas. A quick, delightful stop your guide will point out.

Cusco's great covered food market, under an iron frame attributed to Gustave Eiffel's era — a riot of tropical fruit, cheeses, chocolate, herbs, hanging meat and stalls of fresh juice where locals shop and eat. A cultural feast for curious teenagers and the place to taste your way through the Andes, with plenty of fruit, corn and vegetarian juice bars for meat-free travellers. Go with a guide, keep valuables close, and skip the raw meat aisles.

The city's best museum of the Incas, set in a handsome colonial mansion a block off the plaza — metalwork, mummies, textiles, ceramics and the world's largest collection of queros, the carved wooden ceremonial drinking cups. A calm, well-told introduction that makes the ruins that follow mean far more, and short enough not to tire a multi-generational group. A private curator-led hour turns it into a genuine highlight.

A charming little chocolate house two blocks from the plaza where children and grandparents alike roast, grind and mould their own bars from Peruvian cacao, and sip Inca-style hot chocolate and cacao-tea. A genuinely fun, hands-on hour for a family with kids, and a warm indoor pause on a cold high-altitude afternoon. Free entry to the shop; the hands-on workshops are booked ahead.

The colossal fortress-temple on the hill above Cusco — three tiers of zig-zag ramparts built from limestone blocks, some weighing over 100 tonnes, fitted so tightly the joints defy explanation. It looms over the whole city and hosts the great Inti Raymi sun festival each June. Only a fraction of the original survives, quarried for the colonial city, yet it still astonishes. A private car and guide save the steep climb and bring the stones to life.

A carved limestone outcrop just past Sacsayhuamán — 'zig-zag' in Quechua — riddled with channels, niches and an underground gallery with a stone altar, once a place of ritual and probably of mummification and sacrifice. Small, strange and atmospheric, easily paired with the other three ruins on the hill above the city in a single morning circuit with a driver. The tunnels and carvings intrigue older children.

The 'Red Fort', named for the rosy tint its stone takes at sunset — a compact hilltop complex of terraces, walls and stairways that likely served as a checkpoint or waystation guarding the road into Cusco. It sits right on the Cusco–Pisac road with wide views over the valley, a quick and worthwhile stop on the four-ruins circuit above the city. Best photographed in the late-day light that gives it its name.

The 'Inca Baths' — a beautifully engineered water shrine of stepped terraces, niches and channels fed by a spring that still runs clear through fountains after five centuries, a monument to the Inca reverence for water. It is the highest and gentlest of the four ruins above Cusco, a short level walk from the road. Pair it with Puka Pukara across the way to close a relaxed half-day circuit.

The famous Andean market spilling across Pisac's plaza and lanes — alpaca knits, silver, ceramics and textiles, busiest and most colourful on Sunday when villagers still come down in traditional dress. The best single place in the valley to shop for gifts, with quality that ranges from tourist trinket to genuine craft, so a guide steers you to the real weavers. Handsome, walkable and a natural pairing with the ruins above.

A towering terraced temple-fortress rising in giant steps above the town, crowned by the unfinished Sun Temple whose six colossal pink-granite monoliths were hauled from a quarry across the valley and up the mountainside — an Inca feat that still baffles engineers. It was the site of one of the few Inca victories over the Spanish. The climb is steep but gradual; a guide sets an easy pace and reveals the stories in the stone.

The best-preserved living Inca town anywhere — a grid of cobbled lanes and canchas (walled courtyards) laid out five centuries ago and still inhabited, with water running in the original stone channels down the middle of the streets. Wandering it is the closest you will come to walking through an Inca settlement. It is also the departure point for the Machu Picchu train, so many stay a night in one of its discreet boutique lodges.

A set of vast concentric circular terraces sunk into the earth like a green amphitheatre — an Inca agricultural laboratory where the temperature drops several degrees from the top ring to the bottom, letting them test crops across dozens of microclimates. Strange, beautiful and unlike anything else in the valley. A short, easy walk around the rim; a guide explains the ingenious science behind the shapes.

The valley's largest town and its quiet luxury base — lower and warmer than Cusco at around 2,870 metres, which makes it the doctors' choice for acclimatising with older travellers and children before going higher. Around it lie the valley's finest lodges and haciendas, farm-to-table restaurants and horse ranches. Not a sightseeing stop so much as the calm, oxygen-rich heart from which to explore everything else at an easy pace.

The mineral-striped ridge that went viral — bands of red, gold, turquoise and lavender laid bare across a 5,036-metre peak, framed by glaciers and grazing alpacas. The reward is huge but so is the altitude: the trailhead alone sits higher than any Alpine summit, so proper acclimatisation and a very early, private start beat the crowds and the afternoon cloud. Horses are available for the final climb; not advised for young children or anyone with heart trouble.

The gentler, quieter answer to Vinicunca — three coloured ridges instead of one, a stone forest and glacier views, reached by a short, nearly flat walk from the road rather than a punishing climb. Far fewer people, and far kinder on the lungs and knees, which makes it the sensible choice for a multi-generational group who still want the rainbow-hills spectacle without the ordeal. Still very high; go slowly and go early.

A glacier-fed lake of astonishing turquoise cradled beneath the snows of Mount Salkantay at around 4,200 metres — one of the most beautiful day hikes from Cusco, a steep but short climb to a mirror of ice-melt ringed by peaks. The colour has to be seen to be believed. It is high and the ascent is stiff; horses ease the way up, and a private guided day with an early start keeps it calm and safe.

The Incas' masterpiece of water engineering — a series of grand terraces threaded by stone canals, fountains and channels that still run perfectly, a working monument to their reverence for water and one of the loveliest, least-visited ruins near Cusco. The surrounding village is also famous for slow-roast cuy for those who wish to try it. Quiet, green and easy underfoot, it anchors a rewarding South Valley day away from the crowds.

A rare pre-Inca city — a vast, rigidly gridded settlement of the Wari culture that flourished centuries before the Incas, its high adobe-and-stone walls and hundreds of rooms spread across the plain near the Lucre lake. It gives context most visitors never get: the Andes had great civilisations long before Machu Picchu. Broad and flat to walk, it pairs naturally with Tipón and Andahuaylillas on a South Valley circuit.

venues.n: Andahuaylillas — the Sistine Chapel of the Andes
venues.d: A modest adobe village church, the Church of San Pedro, that hides one of the most dazzling Baroque interiors in the Americas — every surface painted, a gilded altar, a coffered ceiling and murals so rich it earned its nickname. The plain exterior makes the reveal inside all the more astonishing. The jewel of the South Valley and a serene, level stop for grandparents; combine with Tipón and Pikillacta for a full unhurried day.

venues.n: A Despacho Ceremony with an Andean Paqo
venues.d: A traditional offering to Pachamama (Mother Earth) and the Apus (mountain spirits), led by a paqo (Andean priest) who builds a mandala of coca leaves, flowers, seeds and symbols to be burned or buried in a rite of gratitude and reciprocity. Arranged privately and respectfully through a good lodge, it is a quiet, moving encounter with a living faith — not a show — and a way for a family to feel the spirit of the mountains they are travelling through.

Cusco birthed a whole school of colonial painting — Andean artists fusing European religious themes with local colour, gold leaf and hidden Inca symbolism, seen across the Cathedral, the Church of the Society of Jesus on the plaza and the Museo de Arte Religioso. A private art-led morning threads the finest canvases together and reveals the coded resistance in them. Cultured, indoor and gentle — ideal for a rest day between higher exertions.

venues.n: San Pedro (Iglesia de la Compañía) & the Plaza Churches
venues.d: The Church of the Society of Jesus (La Compañía) shares the plaza with the Cathedral and rivals it — a soaring Andean-Baroque façade the Jesuits built to outshine their neighbour, over the palace of the Inca Huayna Capac. Climb to the choir balcony for one of the best views over the square. A short, rewarding stop that completes the plaza and shelters you from the midday sun at altitude.

Cusco sits at 3,400 metres and the treks climb far higher, so the single most important piece of planning is time: spend the first day or two low and slow — many advisors put families in the Sacred Valley (around 2,800m) first and save Cusco and Rainbow Mountain for later. Coca tea, gentle pacing, hydration and bottled oxygen help; a doctor's advice on Diamox and any heart condition is essential before the peaks. Plan the itinerary low-to-high, not the reverse.
A living museum to Peru's national spirit — dozens of piscos and every turn on the pisco sour, with tastings and live music near the Plaza de Armas.
An open-air rooftop high in the San Blas quarter with a wall-to-wall panorama over the red roofs of Cusco — the city's signature sundowner and pisco-sour view.

venues.n: Bar Nazarenas — Palacio Nazarenas, A Belmond Hotel
venues.d: The hushed courtyard bar of the Belmond palace-convent — expert pisco sours and Andean cocktails in one of the city's most refined, hidden settings.
The bar of Gastón Acurio's Cusco restaurant on the Plaza Regocijo — Peru's finest chef's take on the pisco sour and Andean-fruit cocktails, before or after dinner.
In the valley, the best evening drinks are the hotel terraces — the fire-lit lounges and pisco bars of the Urubamba resorts, framed by the Andes at dusk.
